messages.content: Write an internal post about making security everyone's responsibility at a software company. Around 250 words.

**Security is everyone's job, and we keep saying that wrong**

Every company says security is everyone's responsibility. In practice that means the security team writes a policy, the rest of us click through the training, and when something breaks, security gets paged anyway. Shared responsibility without shared capability is just spread-out blame.

Three things change this quarter.

First, security stops being an approval queue. The team is moving to paved paths instead: a secrets manager that's less work than an env file, a dependency bot that opens the PR for you, service templates with auth already wired. If the safe path is slower than the unsafe one, people take the unsafe one, and honestly, they're right to.

Second, threat modeling moves into design review. No separate ceremony, no separate document. Your design doc gets a section on what an attacker would want and how they'd get it. Two paragraphs is enough. The value is in thinking about it while the design is still cheap to change.

Third, incident write-ups belong to the team that owns the code. You know your system better than security does. They'll review the draft and push back on it, but the story is yours to tell.

None of this means you're on your own. #security is staffed during business hours and someone will pair with you on a design or a nasty finding. What we're asking is that you stop treating security as a gate someone else operates, and start treating it as part of the work — the same way you already treat tests and on-call.

Questions, disagreements, better ideas: reply in the thread.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.

Every company repeats that line. What it means in practice: the security team writes a policy, the rest of us click through a training module, and when something breaks, security still gets paged. Responsibility without capability is just blame with a wider blast radius.

Three changes land this quarter.

Security stops running an approval queue. The team is building paved paths instead: a secrets manager that beats an env file for convenience, a dependency bot that opens the PR itself, service templates with auth already wired in. When the safe route costs more time than the unsafe one, people take the unsafe one. They're not wrong to.

Threat modeling joins design review. No new meeting, no new document. Your design doc grows a section on what an attacker wants and how they'd get it. Two paragraphs will do. The point is to think about it while the design is still cheap to change.

Incident write-ups go to the team that owns the code. You understand your system better than security does. They'll read your draft and argue with it, but the account is yours to write.

You won't be alone in any of this. #security is staffed through business hours, and someone will sit down with you over a design or an ugly finding. What we're asking is that you quit treating security as a gate another team operates, and start treating it as part of the job, the way you already treat tests and on-call.

Reply in the thread with questions, objections, or better plans.
